core_principles.text: An upright trunk tends to create a 90/90 lunge where both knees are at 90-degree angles at the bottom of the movement, placing the majority of the upper body weight directly over the hips.
An upright trunk position increases torque on the forward knee, making the movement more quadriceps dominant as the knee extensors bear more responsibility.
Leaning slightly forward with the upper body weight positioned over the mid-thigh distributes demand evenly across the hip, knee, and ankle, which increases gluteus maximus involvement.
To maximize glute involvement, keep the forward heel on the ground while decelerating toward the floor and distribute weight evenly across the forward foot.
Adding trunk rotation toward the forward leg while leaning forward eccentrically loads the gluteus maximus in both the sagittal and transverse planes, further increasing its involvement.
Maintain solid hip-knee-ankle alignment during multiplanar lunges.
Avoid taking strides that are too long to ensure control is maintained throughout the entire range of motion.
Reaching toward the ground with your hands as you step can help soften the landing of each step and reinforce eccentric control.

common_mistakes.text: Lifting the forward heel off the ground while decelerating toward the floor during a lunge.
Taking strides that are too long, which leads to using momentum to propel oneself back up.

consequences.text: Taking a stride that is too long causes the exerciser to rely on momentum to propel themselves up, reducing control throughout the range of motion.
An upright trunk position causes the forward knee to experience more torque because it is the joint farthest from the load of the body.

core_principles.text: Stand with the feet hip-width apart and grip one dumbbell in each hand with the palms facing each other and the arms straight down by the side.
Keep the back straight and step forward with the lead leg.
As the front foot hits the floor, lower the back knee towards the floor.
Descend to a comfortable range of motion.
Push the front foot into the ground to stand up by bringing both feet back together at the starting position.
Have space between your legs to help with balance.
The length of the lunge should be about twice your hip width, as a lunge that is too long may force you to lean forward.
Keep your front foot always on the ground, with the whole foot rooted on the floor.
Keep your body straight at all times, avoiding leaning forward or back when you stand or step.
Keep your front knee behind your toes.

common_mistakes.text: Making the lunge step too short or too long.
Placing the feet on the same line, which reduces stability.
Allowing the front knee to collapse inward.
Having a shaky front knee during the movement.
Allowing the front foot to be unstable on the ground.
Leaning the torso forward or backward.
Making jerky movements, particularly when stepping back.
Allowing the back knee to go too low when the leg lacks the necessary strength.
Aggressively pushing against the ground, particularly when stepping back.
Allowing the front heel to come off the ground, which can happen if the lunge is too short.
Allowing the knees to go over the toes.
Maintaining poor posture during the exercise.

consequences.text: Incorrect lunge technique can lead to knee pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can cause ankle pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can cause foot pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can lead to back pain.
Incorrect lunge technique can cause shoulder pain.
Incorrect lunge technique promotes poor posture.
Incorrect lunge technique results in not training the right muscles and straining others.
